To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We present a simple, practical method for reinforcement learning that can be used to train policies that perform well in target environments with different dynamics.

(i) we propose Off-Dynamics Reinforcement (ODR) learning, a simple, intuitive, practical, and theoretically grounded method for domain adaptation in RL; (ii) ODR is applicable to continuous control tasks and does not require an explicit model of dynamics; and (iii) ODR achieves state-of-the-art results for domain adaptation in continuous control tasks.
we introduce off-dynamics RL, a method for domain adaptation in RL, and that off-dynamics RL achieves state-of-the-art results on a variety of RL benchmarks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of domain adaptation in reinforcement~learning.
the following question: Can we train an agent to solve a task in a target domain, without ever interacting with the target domain, but instead using only interactions with a different, source domain?
the question of whether it is possible to train an agent in a source environment to perform well in a different target environment, even if the dynamics are different.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method is a practical approach to transfer learning that can be used in many different settings.
the proposed method can be used to transfer the knowledge from a source domain to a target domain.
we present a simple and practical method for domain adaptation in RL.

the agent can be trained for transfer in the source domain by modifying the reward to penalize transitions that are more likely to be seen in the source domain than the target domain, and that this modified reward can be estimated by learning auxiliary classifiers for source and target domain transitions.
we are able to train an agent to solve a target task by training it in a different, source, task.

the reward function in RL is not just an indicator of what is good or bad for the agent.
